abstract: Taxonomic identification provides essential information about microalgae, but a shared species assignment does not necessarily imply similar physiological behavior. This study combined microscopy, ribosomal DNA sequencing, and O2 exchange measurements to characterize 20 green microalgal strains, comprising 18 environment-derived and two previously identified model strains. Net O2 evolution and post illumination consumption were measured across 17 increasing irradiances in three independently grown cultures per strain. Maximum differences between pair means for net O2 evolution were 18.12, 7.82, and 10.50 micromol O2 L/min for the Chlorella sorokiniana, Desmodesmus abundans, and Tetradesmus/Acutodesmus obliquus pairs at 100, 50, and 300 micromol photons m/s, respectively; all three cultures of one strain exceeded all three of the other at those irradiances. Within-pair ITS sequences differed by at most one nucleotide over the shared regions. Separately normalized profiles formed five exploratory groups, but group membership was sensitive to culture resampling, the number of principal components, and rate-extraction windows. Physiological distances showed no clear association with 18S patristic distances or assigned genus. Interpretation is limited by provisional species assignments, three cultures per strain, and a single ascending irradiance sequence that confounds light intensity with elapsed time and unmeasured carbon availability. O2 exchange profiling therefore provides complementary information about individual strains under a common experimental protocol, without establishing stable physiological classes or steady-state capacities.
